subject: Civil Engineering
title: Highway Capacity and Bottlenecks
description: Learn Highway Capacity and Bottlenecks in one minute.

hook.text: Add a lane and traffic improves — for a year. Then it fills up again. Why?

buildup.text: Capacity is the maximum flow rate a road can handle — typically 2,200 cars per lane per hour.

discovery.text: Bottlenecks form at lane drops, merges, and weaving sections — flow collapses locally.

twist.text: Induced demand means new capacity attracts new trips — the road fills up again.

climax.text: Houston's Katy Freeway expanded to 26 lanes — commute times still got worse.

punchline.text: You can't build your way out of congestion. The demand always catches up.

quiz.question: What is induced demand in transportation engineering?
options: Traffic caused by construction work on existing roads
New road capacity attracts new trips, filling the road again
Demand created by toll increases on parallel routes

details.summary: Highway capacity is the maximum number of vehicles that can pass a point per hour under prevailing conditions. Bottlenecks, such as lane drops, merges, and steep grades, reduce capacity below the theoretical maximum, creating congestion that often extends far upstream of the restriction.
details.whyItMatters: Identifying and relieving bottlenecks is the most cost-effective way to reduce highway congestion. A single bottleneck can degrade performance for kilometers of otherwise adequate roadway.
takeaways: A typical freeway lane can carry about 2,200 vehicles per hour maximum
Bottlenecks create congestion far upstream of the actual restriction
Lane drops, merges, and grades are the most common bottleneck types

faq.question: What happens to traffic flow at a bottleneck?
faq.answer: When arriving traffic exceeds bottleneck capacity, a queue forms upstream. Vehicles slow and stop in a wave that propagates backward. Downstream of the bottleneck, traffic flows freely at reduced volume. The queue grows until demand drops below capacity.

faq.question: How do engineers increase capacity at highway bottlenecks?
faq.answer: Solutions include adding auxiliary lanes through merging zones, extending acceleration and deceleration lanes, improving sight distance, adding climbing lanes on steep grades, and using ramp metering to control the rate vehicles enter the freeway.
